articles.content: Why Most Dependency Alerts Don’t Matter Kilo Blog Subscribe Sign in Why Most Dependency Alerts Don’t Matter How Kilo Security Agent uses AI reachability analysis to reduce false positives and prioritize exploitable vulnerabilities Brendan O'Leary Jun 24, 2026 6 2 1 Share Last month I heard about an engineer on our team spending forty-five minutes investigating a critical Dependabot alert for a lodash command injection vulnerability. He traced the call paths, read the advisory, and checked our imports. The function wasn’t reachable. Forty-five minutes gone for a single alert out of hundreds. (This engineer may or may not have been me.) This is common across teams using dependency scanners. If you’ve worked at a company that takes security seriously — or one that’s simply turned on Dependabo

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: Every finding gets a transparent four-step trace: found package, reviewed advisory, checked repo usage, and determined reachability. When it says "no reachable risk," you can read exactly why. When a bug is reachable, it can open the remediation PR for you.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: So we built Kilo Security Agent. It syncs your Dependabot alerts, then uses AI static analysis to determine whether each vulnerability is actually exploitable in your specific codebase. A lodash command injection CVE doesn't matter if you never call the vulnerable function with untrusted input.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: GitHub can tell you a CVE exists in lodash 4.17.20. What it can't tell you is whether your code ever touches the affected function. The alert is accurate as metadata. It's useless for prioritization until someone checks reachability by hand.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: Here's the number that reframes it. Endor Labs found fewer than 9.5% of dependency vulnerabilities are actually reachable. Coana puts the false positive rate of conventional SCA tools as high as 95%. Over 90% of what you're triaging is noise.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: This is the Dependabot workflow almost everyone knows. You open the alerts tab, see severity badges stacked across dozens of findings, and have no idea which ones matter. So you investigate all of them, or you start ignoring all of them. Both are bad.

tweets.creator: @kilocode
tweets.text: Most of your Dependabot alerts don't matter, and you're spending real engineering hours proving it one at a time. One of our engineers spent 45 minutes on a single critical alert last week. The vulnerable function was never reachable. The alert was noise.
